extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and scholars of literature, folklore, and anthropology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit criteria for producing creative and ethnographic writing that incorporates folklore, dialect, and performance adaptation — i.e., how to represent, document, and dramatize community-based material in literary and anthropological work. Draws on Hurston's practices, contemporary criticism, and methodological trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent speech patterns of the period
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hurston strove to represent speech patterns of the period, which she had documented through ethnographic research.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base dialogue on documented fieldwork and idiomatic usage; aim for fidelity to how people actually spoke in the community studied. The page notes this approach is rooted in thinking like a folklorist and that critics later praised her "skillful use of idiomatic speech." Anti-pattern: inventing or flattening dialect without field grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of African‑American dialect (authenticity vs. risk of caricature)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The use of African‑American dialect, as featured in Hurston's novels, became less popular. Younger writers felt that it was demeaning... Several of Hurston's literary contemporaries criticized her use of dialect, saying that it was a caricature of African‑American culture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing dialect, weigh authenticity and the writer's documentary basis against possible political and ethical interpretations. Be aware critics may read dialect as 'caricature' or pandering to certain audiences; consider audience, purpose, and historical context to avoid reproducing demeaning tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize folklore for performance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hurston had a strong belief that folklore should be dramatized.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt folk material into staged forms (revues, theater) while preserving authentic songs, dances, and cultural elements. Examples: Her folk revue The Great Day and later From Sun to Sun and Singing Steel featured authentic African song and dance. Anticipate practical constraints (production, audience reception) and maintain cultural respectfulness in performance uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend anthropology, folklore, and personal narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: About Tell My Horse: it is described as “a genre‑defying book that mixes anthropology, folklore, and personal narrative.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermix scholarly observation, folklore transcription, and first‑person narrative to convey rituals and lived experience; genre hybridity can capture atmosphere and participant perspectives. Be transparent about which passages are analysis, which are reportage, and which are literary re‑creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use qualitative ethnographic methods to convey atmosphere and social interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hurston's method of fieldwork was not overly analytical or quantitative... her qualitative ethnographic fieldwork has the ability to convey how the social interactions... and the culture's use of music, are used [to] celebrate the life and afterlife...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize participant observation, narrative description, and experiential detail when the goal is to evoke atmosphere, ritual feeling, and social dynamics. Trade‑off: less formal analysis or tonal/musicological breakdown, but greater capacity to convey lived meaning. Make methodological choices explicit to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for fidelity to original folk tales while navigating external expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Hurston “intended to publish a collection of several hundred folk tales... She wanted to have them be as close to the original as possible but struggled to balance the expectations of her academic adviser... and her patron.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing collected oral material, strive to keep tales close to informants' versions. Expect pressure from editors, patrons, or academic advisers to shape material for particular audiences; document editorial changes and the provenance of versions. Preserve originals where possible (transcripts, recordings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and archive field materials (audio, film, photographs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes Hurston “took photographs of [Cudjoe Lewis] and others in the community, and recorded the only known film footage of him” and that sound recordings and film were part of her collected material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect multimodal documentation (audio recordings, film, photographs, transcripts) to preserve informants' voices and contexts for future scholarship and publication. Archive materials with reliable provenance and institutional repositories to ensure long‑term access (as happened with posthumous publications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give proper attribution and avoid plagiarism in reporting field subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: On an article about Cudjoe Lewis: “According to her biographer Robert E. Hemenway, this piece largely plagiarized the work of Emma Langdon Roche... Hurston did add new information...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge prior published sources and the contributions of earlier researchers and informants. When incorporating others' published material, cite appropriately; when adding new field data, clearly indicate original contributions. Failure to attribute can undermine credibility and ethical standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authentic local settings as literary terrain
rubrics_metrics.description: Hurston “later used Eatonville as the setting for many of her stories” and described it as a place where African Americans could live independent of white society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on familiar localities and community knowledge to ground fiction in specific place; use setting to explore social life and identity. Ensure representations honor community complexity rather than flattening it into stereotype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of thematic clarity and political expectations in African‑American writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Richard Wright's criticism: “The sensory sweep of her novel carries no theme, no message, no thought... her novel is not addressed to the Negro, but to a white audience...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that contemporaries may evaluate works by the presence or absence of an explicit political message or thematic argument. Authors should decide whether to foreground social/political aims or to prioritize aesthetic/documentary concerns, and be prepared for divergent critical responses depending on that choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful, early use of ethnomusicological methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Hurston's Tell My Horse “explored ethnomusicological methods of study long before there were formal boundaries for the discipline, especially not boundaries that included the respectful study of communities of color.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting music and ritual, adopt respectful, community‑centered practices and acknowledge informants' expertise. Even before formal disciplinary norms, prioritize respectful study over exploitative extraction; include contextual interpretation alongside musical documentation.
